---
title: Derived B-rep
description: Faces, edges and corners read off the field rather than stored — exact, differentiable, and the input to STEP export, dragging, and a better tet mesh.
---

cadjoint models implicitly, so it stores no boundary representation. It does
not need to: it can *derive* one, and the derivation is differentiable.

Every hard primitive is a `min`/`max` over smooth **patch fields** with exact
surface ownership — a box is six planes, a cylinder is one cylinder and two
caps, a revolved profile is one surface per profile edge. A face is the part of
one patch's zero set that survived the booleans; an edge is where two patch
zero sets meet; a vertex is where three do. Each of those is the solution of a
small system in the design parameters, and each differentiates by the implicit
function theorem. *Which* patches meet is discrete and frozen per extraction;
*where* they meet is continuous and exact.

That one observation is what lets three products share almost all of their
code:

| Product | Module | What it adds to the graph |
|---|---|---|
| Exact STEP / OBJ / STL export | `cadjoint.brep.step` | surfaces, curves, simplified loops |
| A draggable B-rep | `cadjoint.brep.drag` | ∂(vertex)/∂(design), with the sketch constraints held |
| A differentiable tet mesh | `cadjoint.brep.plc`, `cadjoint.brep.mesh_gmsh` | node ownership, so every node moves by its own projection |

All three go through one kernel, `cadjoint.brep.project`, which is the only
place a position is computed. The viewer's feature-edge overlay is the fourth
consumer: every edge it draws is a `BRepEdge`.

## The kernel

A face point solves `f_a(x) = 0`; an edge point solves `f_a(x) = f_b(x) = 0`;
a vertex solves three. All of them are the same minimum-norm Gauss–Newton step,
`x ← x − Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹ f(x)`, which at one field is exactly the step
`cadjoint.fem.motion.project_points` takes. The forward iteration runs on
`stop_gradient` values and a `custom_vjp` attaches the implicit-function
adjoint: a seed's *tangential* placement does not affect the answer — the seed
chooses the branch, never the position on it — which is the frozen-topology
contract stated as a derivative. Where the fields are not transversal (a
tangent pair, a blend) the step is suppressed in both passes and the point
carries no parameter derivative.

## Extract a graph

`extract_brep` dual-contours the scene on a grid — that pass is *discovery*,
not geometry — asks which patch owns each surface point, groups same-owner
quads into faces, chains the boundaries into edges, and then re-solves every
mesh vertex against its owners at its own arity.

```python
from cadjoint.brep import extract_brep
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec
from cadjoint.sdf.boolean import Difference
from cadjoint.sdf.primitives import Box, Cylinder

bore = Scalar(0.25, free=True, name="bore")
plate = Difference((Box([0.6, 0.6, 0.4]), Cylinder(radius=bore, height=1.0)),
                   smoothness=0.0)

grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-0.8, -0.8, -0.6), (1.6, 1.6, 1.2), 20)
brep = extract_brep(plate, grid)

report = brep.report()
print(report["faces"], report["edges"], report["vertices"], report["face_kinds"])
# 7 14 8 {'plane': 6, 'cylinder': 1}
```

That is the textbook B-rep of a plate with a hole — six planes and one
cylinder, twelve straight edges and two rim circles, eight corners — and it is
exact: the corners land on `(±0.6, ±0.6, ±0.4)` to better than 1e-9 and the
fitted bore radius is `0.250000006`. Extract on a shifted lattice and the same
7 / 14 / 8 come out; topology is discovered, not sampled.

Surface *type* is structural, read off the primitive's own patch ordering,
never guessed from a point cloud. Only the placement is fitted, and every fit
carries its measured residual:

```python
for face in brep.analytic_faces():
    s = face.surface
    print(face.kind, s.radius, s.residual)
# plane    0.0  0.0
# cylinder 0.250000006  1.3e-08
# ...
```

What the graph holds:

| | Fields |
|---|---|
| `BRepFace` | `kind` (`plane`, `cylinder`, `sphere`, `cone`, `blend`), `analytic`, `surface` (an `AnalyticSurface` with origin, axis, radius, residual and a `sense` that says whether it is a bore), `quads`, `loops`, `area` |
| `BRepEdge` | the two `faces` and `patches` it separates, a `polyline` re-solved by the two-field projection, its endpoint `vertices`, `closed`, `analytic`, `residual` |
| `BRepVertex` | the incident `faces`, the three `patches` solved for, the solved `point`, `analytic`, `residual` |
| `BRep` | those three lists plus `points`, `owner_patches` and `owner_arity` per mesh vertex, the `mesh` and `grid` it was discovered on, and `stats` |

### Blends are found exactly

A smooth union creates surface that lies on *no* patch's zero set. The test is
thresholdless: at a surface point the owning patch's value is zero if the patch
really owns it and of order the blend radius if the point is on a fillet, so
`blend_tolerance` — a thousandth of the grid diagonal by default — separates
the two without an angle to tune. Blend faces are real faces with `kind ==
"blend"`; they are never mistaken for geometry, and `stats` counts what they
cost: on the starter's thermal body 13 of 58 faces are blend, and every edge
bordering one has no exact curve. That is the graph's one real limitation,
and [the architecture note](../research/brep-architecture.md) §9.3 sets out
the way past it.

## Export

`save_brep_step` writes STEP AP214, analytic where the graph can certify it: a
planar face becomes a `PLANE` trimmed by its own loops (holes included), a
full cylindrical band bounded by two rim circles becomes a
`CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE` with `CIRCLE` edges, and everything else — blends above
all — is faceted so that the shell always closes.

```python
from cadjoint.brep import save_brep_obj, save_brep_step, save_brep_stl

report = save_brep_step(brep, "plate.step")
print(report["faces"], report["entities"])
# {'plane': 6, 'cylinder': 1, 'facet': 0, 'dropped': 0} 181

save_brep_obj(brep, "plate.obj")
save_brep_stl(brep, "plate.stl")
```

181 entities against roughly ten thousand for the same plate from
`meshing.export.save_step`; and where the faceted file's volume is 1.6e-3 off
because a 28-gon stands in for the bore, the analytic one is right to 1e-7 —
there is no discretization left. OCCT reads both as one valid solid
(`tests/brep/test_step_kernel.py`, with the `stepcheck` extra).

One rule decides what may be exact: **every face sharing a boundary must make
the same decision**. A loop simplified on one side and not the other, or a
circle on one side and a polygon on the other, splits the shared edge and the
shell does not sew — both were found by asking OCCT — so analytic treatment is
refused for any loop that touches a vertex a faceted face still uses.

## Drag

A stored B-rep lets you drag a vertex because the vertex *is* the geometry.
Here the vertex is the solution of three equations, so dragging is an inverse
problem: find the parameter update that moves the solution to the target
without breaking the sketch's constraints. One Gauss–Newton step stacks the
handle row on the constraint rows and takes the minimum-norm least-squares
answer, so the smallest edit that does both is the one chosen; a final
projection restores the constraints exactly.

```python
import numpy as np
from cadjoint.brep import drag_handle, extract_brep
from cadjoint.construction import PolygonProfile, extrude
from cadjoint.geometry import Scalar
from cadjoint.meshing import GridSpec

depth = Scalar(0.8, free=True, name="depth")
profile = PolygonProfile([[-1.0, -0.5], [1.0, -0.5], [1.0, 0.5], [-1.0, 0.5]],
                         name="slab")
slab = extrude(profile, depth=depth)

slab_grid = GridSpec.from_bounds((-1.3, -0.8, -0.7), (2.6, 1.6, 1.4), (26, 16, 14))
slab_brep = extract_brep(slab, slab_grid)

points = np.array([v.point for v in slab_brep.vertices])
top = int(np.argmax(points.sum(axis=1)))            # the (1, 0.5, 0.4) corner

result = drag_handle(slab, slab_brep, "vertex", top,
                     points[top] + [0.0, 0.0, 0.05], apply=False)
print(result.error, result.moved)
# 1.2e-08 [('depth', 0.1)]
```

The corner rides at `depth / 2`, so lifting it by 0.05 is a depth change of
0.1 — and that is the only parameter that moved, although the four profile
vertices were free too. Drag the same corner sideways and `slab_v2`, the one
sketch point that owns it, moves by exactly the drag. `apply=True` writes the
solved parameters back into the scene.

Two things the drag refuses rather than fakes. A move that would take the
handle off the solid's boundary — burying the corner in the deck — is a
topology change the frozen graph cannot represent; the result comes back with
`topology_changed=True`, `applied=False` and a reason, and the parameters are
returned for the caller to decide. And each call moves at most `max_step`
(half a cell diagonal by default, the same clamp every projection uses), so a
drag longer than that lands short unless you raise the clamp or take it in
steps — which is what a UI drag is anyway.

`∂(handle)/∂θ` is not a single `jax.jacrev`: a profile's winding is a discrete
fact, read concretely, so the kernel's Jacobian in the *point* is autodiff and
the parameter sensitivity of the field values is central differences on the
three scalars — 2·dof field evaluations, not 2·dof Newton solves.

## Meshing from the graph

Today's tet path hands TetGen the dual-contour quads. The graph offers two
better inputs.

**The same TetGen, fed the graph.** `brep_plc` re-triangulates planar faces
from their simplified loops and tags every node with its owner patch set, so
`recompute_plc_points` moves each node by its own arity when the design
changes. Fed to TetGen with the same bounds as `sdf_to_tet_mesh`, every quality
metric improves a little (creases land exactly on their creases). Back on the
plate with the bore:

```python
from cadjoint.brep import brep_plc, plc_tet_mesh
from cadjoint.fem import tet_radius_ratios

plc = brep_plc(brep)
tets = plc_tet_mesh(brep, plc)            # a cadjoint.fem.TetMesh
print(tets.points.shape, tets.cells.shape)
print(float(tet_radius_ratios(tets.points, tets.cells[:, :4]).min()))
```

Coarsening the planar faces all the way to their loops works — 27× fewer
surface triangles for a bit-identical volume on the fin comb — but only on
faces whose every neighbour can coarsen too, and a blend face pins the boundary
of every face it touches. A blended body therefore cannot be coarsened at all
yet; the number is in the note, and so is the fix.

**Gmsh, fed the exact STEP.** `gmsh_tet_mesh` writes the analytic STEP,
lets Gmsh (HXT, second order) size the elements by the *part* rather than by
the lattice, and reads back, for every node, which CAD entity owns it.
`assign_ownership` matches that entity to a `BRepFace`, so midside nodes sit
on the true cylinder rather than at the chord midpoint a straight-sided
promotion gives, and every node moves under a design change by the same
projection as everything else:

```python
from cadjoint.brep.mesh_gmsh import gmsh_available, gmsh_tet_mesh, tet_mesh_from_gmsh

if gmsh_available():                      # uv sync --extra gmsh
    gm = gmsh_tet_mesh(brep, target_size=0.16)
    print(gm.stats["nodes"], gm.stats["cells"], gm.stats["arity_counts"])
    # 2726 1405 {0: 1098, 1: 1424, 2: 196, 3: 8}

    tets = tet_mesh_from_gmsh(brep, gm)   # the same TetMesh layout tet10_mesh builds
    print(tets.order, tets.cells.shape)   # 2 (1405, 10)
```

On the plate this is 0.26 s against 2.08 s for the dual-contour route, with the
worst radius ratio 7.5× better; a mesh-volume derivative with respect to the
bore radius matches central differences to 1e-12. Neither figure counts
`extract_brep`, which only this route needs and which costs more than either —
the route pays off where the graph is already being built for the exporter or
the drag handles.

Gmsh is GPL-2.0-or-later and cadjoint is Apache-2.0, so nothing under
`cadjoint/` imports it at module scope. The supported route is the
`cadjoint_tet_gmsh` image, a [plugin](plugins.qmd) of kind `tet_mesher` where
the licence boundary is a process boundary; `gmsh_tet_mesh(..., plugin=...)`
sends the STEP there instead of to an in-process Gmsh. `pip install
'cadjoint[gmsh]'` links it into your own process, a choice to make knowingly.
A `mesher="gmsh"` keyword on `SimMesh` is proposed, not shipped.

## Where it is used today

- **The playground's feature edges** are `BRepEdge`s: `_mesh_edge_payload`
  extracts the graph on the viewport's 64³ grid and draws every analytic edge
  resampled at half a cell and re-projected, so a bore rim is a circle to
  5e-8 wherever the grid falls, and curves meet at their corners. It sets
  `blend_tolerance` to one cell, so a fillet finer than the overlay can show is
  drawn as the edge it rounds. See [the playground](viewer.qmd#rendering).
- **STEP export** from the playground and from a script goes through
  `save_brep_step` when you want faces, and through `meshing.export.save_step`
  when you want the mesh as it is.

## What is honest about being a prototype

- Analytic STEP covers `PLANE` and `CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE`. Spheres and cones are
  classified — the graph knows, with a residual — but not emitted, because
  their trimming curves are neither lines nor circles.
- Two curved surfaces meet in a curve the graph *has* as a polyline to 3e-8,
  but STEP wants a curve; marching it and fitting a B-spline is the next step.
- Lofts have no patch decomposition yet and come out as one `freeform` face.
- Extraction is eager-mode JAX dispatch: 3–4 s for the plate at 20³, ~18 s
  for the starter's thermal body at 40³. The kernel's loops are fixed-shape
  and jittable, and the overlay's batched programs are the first step down
  that road.
